title: Definite integrals and their properties
objective: Evaluate a definite integral from an antiderivative, use the properties of definite integrals, and split an integral where the expression inside an absolute value changes sign.

blocks.text: The definite integral of f(x) from a to b is F(b) − F(a), where F is an antiderivative of f. The numbers a and b are the lower and upper limits of integration.

When f(x) lies above the x-axis, the definite integral is the area under the curve between the lines x = a and x = b. It is the limit of the sum of Riemann: the total area of thin strips of width Δx and height f(xᵢ).
No constant of integration is written in a definite integral, because it cancels: (F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c) = F(b) − F(a). An integral whose two limits are equal is zero.

Properties. Swapping the limits changes the sign of the integral (permutation of bounds). For any c between a and b, the integral from a to b is the integral from a to c plus the integral from c to b (Chasles relation). If f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b] with a ≤ b, the integral is not negative, and if f(x) ≤ g(x) there, the integral of f is at most the integral of g.

To integrate an absolute value such as |x − 1|, find where the expression inside changes sign, split the interval there with the Chasles relation, and on each part replace the absolute value by the expression or by its opposite.
